title: Improved Quantum Random Self-Reduction for Linear Problems
authors: Vahid R. Asadi, Shuichi Hirahara, Nobutaka Shimizu
abstract: We study quantum random self-reductions for linear problems over finite fields. Let $M\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}$ be an arbitrary matrix, and let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle that agrees with the linear map $x\mapsto Mx$ on an $\varepsilon$-fraction of inputs $x\sim\mathbb{F}^n$. Given coherent access to $\mathcal{O}$ and coherent entry access to $M$, we give a uniform quantum reduction that computes $Mx$ on any prescribed input $x$ with probability at least $2/3$ in time $\widetilde{O}(nT^{1/3})$, for $n\le T\le n^{3/2}$ and constant field size and $\varepsilon$, where $T$ is the cost of one coherent query to $\mathcal{O}$. In particular, when $T=\widetilde{O}(n)$, the reduction runs in time $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$, improving the $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2}+T)$ reduction of Asadi, Golovnev, Gur, Shinkar, and Subramanian (SODA 2024).   Our reduction uses the Bogolyubov--Ruzsa subspace guaranteed by additive combinatorics, but it avoids learning this subspace explicitly, which was computationally expensive for the previous reduction; in particular, it does not recover a basis for its orthogonal complement. The main technical step is to decompose the inputs into sparse pieces and find a vector that lies outside the Bogolyubov--Ruzsa subspace via a quantum search based on amplitude amplification. This yields a tunable tradeoff between the cost of querying the average-case oracle and the cost of verifying matrix-vector products.
summary: This paper presents an improved quantum random self-reduction for solving linear problems over finite fields when the underlying linear map is only accessible via an imperfect oracle. By utilizing the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa subspace and quantum search techniques, the authors achieve a time complexity of $\widetilde{O}(n T^{1/3})$, which is a substantial improvement over existing quantum bounds.
main_problem: The paper addresses the development of quantum random self-reductions to solve linear problems over finite fields when access to the underlying linear map is only available on a small fraction of inputs.
main_result: A uniform quantum reduction is established that computes the matrix-vector product $Mx$ with high probability in time $\widetilde{O}(n T^{1/3})$, significantly improving upon previous bounds.
method: The reduction leverages the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa subspace from additive combinatorics and employs quantum search techniques based on amplitude amplification to avoid explicitly learning the subspace structure.
model_or_system: The model is an abstract computational setting involving a linear map $M \in \mathbb{F}^{n 	imes n}$ and an imperfect oracle $\mathcal{O}$ that provides access to $Mx$ only on an $\epsilon$-fraction of inputs.
key_observables: The primary observable is the success probability of computing $Mx$ for an arbitrary input $x$, which is maintained at at least $2/3$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the dimension $n$, the query cost $T$ of the oracle, and the error fraction $\epsilon$. The running time depends critically on the relationship between $n$ and $T$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes constant field size and a fixed error fraction $\epsilon$. The improvements rely on avoiding computationally expensive steps like explicitly recovering a basis for the orthogonal complement of the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa subspace.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the derived running time bound, $e^{O(n T^{1/3})}$, against the running times of prior state-of-the-art reductions across different regimes of $T$.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon previous work by first establishing the necessary theoretical tools (like the BR subspace) and then constructing a multi-stage quantum algorithm. This involves defining an amplified oracle $\mathcal{O}'$, using it to build a 'BR table,' and finally executing a quantum search procedure to achieve the desired complexity bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides a significant theoretical advancement in the complexity of quantum algorithms for solving average-case problems, demonstrating a superior time complexity compared to prior quantum reductions in the field.
